title: He Vanished in a Sahara Sandstorm. 9 Days Later He Walked Out in Another Country
description:
Case 008, the full case file. April 1994: Mauro Prosperi, an Italian police officer and pentathlete, was one of about eighty runners in the Marathon des Sables, a six-day race of about 250 km across the Moroccan Sahara in which every runner carries his own food. On the fourth and longest stage a sandstorm hit. By his account it lasted eight hours and he kept moving so the sand would not bury him; when it cleared, the marked trail was gone. He saved his urine in a spare bottle, waited as the race rules said, and fired his flare at a search helicopter that never saw him. He sheltered in an abandoned Muslim shrine (a marabout), put a small Italian flag on its roof and, by his own account, killed about twenty bats and drank their blood. An aeroplane also passed without seeing him. At his lowest point he expected to die there; he did not, and he set out for distant mountains, walking in the cool of morning and evening, eating beetles, lizards and a snake and squeezing plants for moisture. On the eighth day he reached an oasis; the next day a young girl herding goats found him. Her Tuareg family gave him goat's milk and took him by camel to a village, and he was taken to hospital in Tindouf, Algeria, 291 km (181 miles) from where he vanished and about 15 kg lighter. He could not eat solid food for months and took almost two years to recover.

His story has been questioned: the race's founder told a magazine in 1998 that it was a fabrication and physically impossible. Others who looked into it, including a film crew that retraced his route and a doctor who writes about survival at the extremes, concluded that he was telling the truth. Prosperi has always stood by it. He went back to the race four years later, dropped out with a toe injury, and returned again to finish it. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The figures who stand in for the race's founder and the doctor are not likenesses of anyone.

source_notes:
LONG-FORM RUN (14 Nov 2026). How the added facts were checked: this session's network policy blocked every direct page fetch (Wikipedia, OffGrid, BBC, ABC, Trail Runner all refused), so nothing was read page by page. The added facts were checked through web-search result summaries of the pages listed in 'sources', on top of the Short's run, which did open Wikipedia, History.com, OffGrid and ExplorersWeb (its notes follow below unchanged). Anything a search could not confirm was left out of the script. The BBC Magazine interview of 2014 was again not readable and is not used. Added facts and where the summaries placed them: about eighty runners, start at Foum Zguid on 10 April 1994 (Wikipedia, Yabiladi); every runner carries his own food (Wikipedia, Marathon des Sables); the fourth stage was the longest, 'over 85 km' in one account, so the script says 'more than eighty'; 'near the front' covers both his placing in Wikipedia's narrative (fourth) and in his own quote (seventh); the storm lasted eight hours and he kept moving for fear of being buried (Wikipedia; Yabiladi gives eight hours 'according to him'; one blog says twelve) so the film says 'by his account' and the run_blind shot carries that label; he saved urine in a spare bottle, a trick from his grandfather (the search summaries attribute this to the All That's Interesting and AOL retellings; Wikipedia, OffGrid and History say he drank it); the race rule was to stay put and wait (Wikipedia); the helicopter and the flare (Wikipedia, OffGrid); a small Italian flag on the shrine roof (Wikipedia; ABC has him hang it from a pole); about twenty bats (HowStuffWorks: 'at least 20', in his own account), killed with a pocket knife (Wikipedia), eaten raw so as not to lose moisture (OffGrid): the narration says only 'kills about twenty of them, and drinks their blood. Raw', nothing of it is shown beyond a hand closing on a bat, and the count card says BY HIS OWN ACCOUNT; an aeroplane that did not spot him (ABC); toward the mountains, walking early and late (Wikipedia, OffGrid); beetles, lizards, snakes and liquid squeezed from plant roots (Wikipedia); an oasis by the eighth day (Wikipedia, OffGrid, Vocal); the girl, the Tuareg family, goat's milk, by camel to a village (Wikipedia, OffGrid, Vocal); military police and hospital in Tindouf, 291 km / 181 miles off course (Wikipedia); weight lost 15 kg (Wikipedia), 16 kg (one account in the search results, not identified with certainty), 35 lb (OffGrid, History), so 'about fifteen kilos'; no solid food for months and almost two years to recover (search summaries; the individual pages behind each phrase could not be identified with certainty); the founder, Patrick Bauer, told Men's Journal in 1998 the story was a fabrication and physiologically impossible (Men's Journal, Wikipedia, OffGrid): he is not named in the narration, his words are paraphrased except the two stamps 'A FABRICATION' and 'PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE', which follow the reported wording; a film crew that retraced the route reported finding the shrine, his belongings and bat skeletons (Wikipedia and OffGrid, read by the Short's run; this run's searches did not re-confirm it, so the script says 'reported finding'); Dr Kenneth Kamler, in Surviving the Extremes, vouches for the account (OffGrid): he is not named or quoted, the script says he 'concluded he was telling the truth'; race safety rules were tightened afterwards (Wikipedia); he returned in 1998 and dropped out with a toe injury (OffGrid, History, a French account 'four years later'); that he later finished is agreed, the year is not (13th in 2001 per Wikipedia, 'completed the race in 2012' per OffGrid and History), so no year is given. Left out on purpose, as in the Short: at the shrine he tried to end his life (all sources). The 'low' segment says only that it was his lowest point, that he decided he was going to die there and thought about his wife, and that he did not die; the method is not stated or shown, Rook makes no joke in it, and the shot is a man sitting with his head down. Also left out because this run could not confirm them: a note to his wife, a second sandstorm, the girl running away, the blindfold, the phone call home, his wife's name and the number of his children, a compass and map, how much water he had left (the script says only that it was running out). Dramatised, not reported, in addition to the Short's list: the bivouac, its tents and the kit table (plain, no logos; that the kit included food, bottles, a flare and a flag is sourced, the rest is set dressing); the checkpoint and its officials; the dune where he wakes; the bottle on the rock; the inside of the shrine (pillars, niche, rugs, the tally marks Rook scratches); the look of the aeroplane and the cloth he waves; the dry riverbed and its ledge; the pool, palms and reeds of the oasis; the camels, the village and its people, the jeep and its driver (sources say military police took him to Tindouf; the vehicle is a stand-in); the ward, the drip, the soup and the spoon; the man with crossed arms behind a desk (a stand-in for the race's founder: no likeness, no dialogue); the film crew's look and equipment and the small bones Rook inspects; the doctor at his desk (a stand-in: no likeness, no dialogue); the toe scene; the finish under the same arch (the real finish line is not depicted); every chart, clock, scale and calendar (illustrations of the sourced figures, not data); and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone.

SHORT'S NOTES (r008-prosperi): Read for this run: Wikipedia (Mauro Prosperi; it leans on a 1998 Men's Journal feature and a 2014 BBC interview), History.com ('5 Stunning Real-Life Survival Stories', updated 2025), RECOIL OFFGRID (Patrick McCarthy, 'Alone in the Sahara', 2018, which quotes the Men's Journal piece and Kenneth Kamler's book) and ExplorersWeb ('More Great Survival Stories', 2020). The BBC Magazine interview of November 2014 could not be opened by this run and is not used or listed; it is known here only second-hand. Agreed by the sources that mention each point: Italian police officer; the 1994 Marathon des Sables in Morocco, a six-day race (History), 251 km / 156 miles (Wikipedia, OffGrid; ExplorersWeb says 233 km, so the insert says 'ABOUT 250 KM'); he went astray on the fourth and longest stage, 14 April (Wikipedia, OffGrid); a sandstorm disoriented him and he kept moving in it (Wikipedia: 'I kept running'; OffGrid has him backtracking afterwards); a search helicopter passed without seeing him (Wikipedia, OffGrid); he sheltered in an abandoned Muslim shrine / marabout (all four); he ate bats there (all four) and drank or sucked their blood (Wikipedia, ExplorersWeb; OffGrid and History say only that he ate them raw); he then walked toward distant mountains in the early morning and evening (Wikipedia, OffGrid) eating beetles, lizards and snakes (Wikipedia; 'insects and reptiles' in History); he was found by a young girl tending goats, part of a Tuareg family who gave him goat's milk (Wikipedia, OffGrid; 'a young girl' in ExplorersWeb; History mentions only a village); he was in Algeria, 291 km / 181 miles off course (Wikipedia), 180 miles from where he disappeared (OffGrid, History), 'almost 300 km' (ExplorersWeb); he later returned to the race (six more times, 13th in 2001, per Wikipedia; 'completed the race in 2012' per OffGrid and History). Where the sources differ: (1) Age in 1994: 38 (Wikipedia, born July 1955) or 39 (OffGrid, History); no age is given in the film. (2) 'Pentathlete' (Wikipedia) or 'former Olympic pentathlete' (OffGrid); the film says only 'pentathlete'. (3) His race position: fourth (Wikipedia's narrative) or seventh (his own quote); not stated. (4) How long: he reached an oasis 'by the eighth day' and met the girl the next day (Wikipedia), 'after eight days' then the girl (OffGrid), 'for nine days he walked' (History), 'lost for nine days' (ExplorersWeb); the script says 'nine days later' and 'Day nine'. (5) Weight lost: 15 kg (Wikipedia), 35 lb (OffGrid, History), 18 kg (ExplorersWeb); no figure is given. (6) The helicopter is in Wikipedia (at sunset) and OffGrid (in the afternoon); the flare he fired at it is in Wikipedia only, so it appears on screen but is not narrated. (7) Rescue route: by camel to a village and then military police and a hospital in Tindouf (Wikipedia, OffGrid), 'an Algerian military camp' (ExplorersWeb), 'flown to a hospital' (History); the film stops at the tent. (8) The account is disputed: the race's founder, Patrick Bauer, called it a fabrication and 'physiologically impossible' (Men's Journal 1998, via Wikipedia and OffGrid) and some physiologists doubted it; against that, a 1995 film crew is reported to have found the shrine, his belongings and bat skeletons (Wikipedia, OffGrid) and Kamler's book concludes he did not lie (OffGrid). Because the bat detail rests on his own telling, the shot carries the label 'BY HIS OWN ACCOUNT' and the description says the story has been questioned. Left out on purpose: at the shrine he tried to end his life (all four sources); a Short for a general audience is not the place for it and nothing in the film alludes to it. Also left out: drinking his own urine (Wikipedia, OffGrid, History), the body of a holy man in the shrine (Wikipedia, from the BBC interview), the second aircraft and second storm, the blindfolded ride with military police, and the damage to his liver. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the runner (white cap, red pack, plain orange bib with no number or sponsor), the start arch, tents and marker flags (plain, no lettering or logos), the helicopter's colours, the shape of the shrine and its tower, the number of bats, the hand taking a bat, a lizard and a beetle (he ate them; how he caught them is not described), the hoof prints, the girl's and the older woman's clothes and the tent (sources say only a Tuareg girl, her grandmother and a tent), the bowl, the closing shot of him back on the start line, the steel flask Rook keeps (he carried water bottles; the flask is a stand-in), both maps (marked as sketches; the border and routes are not to scale), the six stage bars (only day four being the longest is sourced) and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet (16:9) reviewed in two full rounds with fixes after each (round 1: 17 shots restaged: kit table, checkpoint, the bottle shot, the wait on the dune, shrine interior, the low-point shot's light and Rook's place in it, the dry riverbed, the snake, the root shot, the oasis camera, the ward's exposure, the finish line, one re-framed repeat that looked into a wall; round 2: sitting poses that read as standing were turned or replaced, the snake recoloured, the thumbnail reframed so the hook sits inside the frame and off the subjects), a composited still per shot to check inserts, overlays, captions and HUD, then a full-length low-resolution rehearsal (384x216, 4 samples, all 2263 3D frames) composited with sound and reviewed at one frame every 1.5 s as round 3, after which six inserts were re-laid out (text clipped at the right edge while popping in, the final board's photo) and the composite was rebuilt and re-checked. The rehearsal passed the automated gate locally both times: 88 shots, mean 2.21 s, longest 3.52 s, loudness -15.1 LUFS, true peak -2.2 dBFS, voice 12.7 dB over the bed, host in 41/88 shots (47%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.78. Audio was measured, not listened to. The full-resolution render and the final gate run in the cloud. Build note: this world file builds its primitives straight from mesh data instead of through Blender operators (same geometry, checked vertex for vertex), because the operator route took over ten minutes to build a scene of 3,800 objects; the build now takes about nine seconds.
